story.title: Up the Steep Slopes of Wilayat Nakhal, the Mountain Road to Wakan and Al Foorah Begins Its Long-Awaited Paving
story.seo_title: Paving the 8.7 km Mountain Road to Wakan and Al Foorah
story.meta_description: Work begins on an OMR 6M+ 8.7-kilometer paved mountain road with 220 streetlights and 37 culverts linking Wakan and Al Foorah in Wilayat Nakhal.

detail.extracted_title: Up the Steep Slopes of Wilayat Nakhal, the Mountain Road to Wakan and Al Foorah Begins Its Long-Awaited Paving
detail.excerpt: Across 8.7 kilometers of rugged Western Hajar rock, engineers have begun paving the mountain route to Wakan and Al Foorah—adding 37 flood culverts and 220 streetlights for village families and hikers.
detail.article_html:
Anyone who has driven up Wadi Mistal toward the high mountain village of Wakan in Wilayat Nakhal remembers the exact moment the asphalt used to end. From the valley floor, the track climbed sharply up the dark limestone wall of the Western Hajar—a steep, winding ribbon of loose gravel and dust where four-wheel-drive gears whined around every hairpin turn. At the top, 2,000 meters above sea level, terraced orchards of pomegranates, apricots, and grapes looked out across the canyon.

This week, heavy excavators began cutting and grading the rock face as construction officially started on the paving of the mountain road leading to both Wakan village and neighboring Al Foorah village in South Al Batinah Governorate. Executed in implementation of Royal Directives to develop Wakan village and upgrade its core services, the project represents an investment of more than OMR 6 million.

Engineering an 8.7-Kilometer Mountain Corridor

Building a durable road in the Western Hajar requires working with the mountain's seasonal water flow as much as its rock slopes. According to H.E. Eng. Masoud bin Said Al Hashmi, Governor of South Al Batinah, the project spans a total length of 8.7 kilometers: a 6.5-kilometer main road ascending to Wakan alongside a 2.2-kilometer link road connecting Al Foorah and surrounding mountain hamlets.

Because heavy winter and summer rains can send sudden torrents rushing down the canyon ravines, the engineering plan includes 37 reinforced box culverts designed to channel wadi water safely beneath the roadbed without washing out the mountain pass. Alongside the asphalt surface, crews are installing 220 streetlights along the full length of the climb, reinforced retaining walls, and mountain safety barriers tailored to the steep terrain.

Everyday Relief for Two Mountain Communities

While thousands of visitors make the trip to Wakan each winter and spring to walk the stone steps between blooming apricot trees and falaj channels, the road's primary impact belongs to the families who live on the mountain year-round.

H.E. Sheikh Khalifa bin Saleh Al Busaidi, Wali of Nakhal, noted that connecting Wakan and Al Foorah with an all-weather paved road directly answers the daily transport needs of residents—from school commutes and medical trips down to Nakhal town to the movement of farm harvests and building supplies. Eng. Nasser Al Balushi, Director of Nakhal Municipality, added that every stage of the alignment has been designed to respect the geological and environmental character of the mountain slopes, ensuring that one of Oman's most cherished high-altitude villages becomes safer to reach without losing the quiet calm that defines life above the clouds.

  • Oman Daily
detail.instagram_caption:
High in the Western Hajar mountains of Wilayat Nakhal, construction and paving works have begun on the steep mountain road leading to the villages of Wakan and Al Foorah in South Al Batinah Governorate. Implemented under Royal Directives to develop Wakan village and upgrade essential infrastructure for residents and visitors, the project carries a total value exceeding OMR 6 million.

The mountain corridor spans 8.7 kilometers in total, comprising a 6.5-kilometer main road ascending to Wakan and a 2.2-kilometer link road connecting neighboring Al Foorah and nearby hamlets. To protect the route against seasonal wadi flash floods and steep mountain gradients, engineers are constructing 37 reinforced box culverts for water drainage alongside 220 streetlights and full traffic safety barriers.

For the mountain families who tend terraced orchards of pomegranates and apricots high above Wadi Mistal, as well as the hikers drawn to Wakan's cool mountain air, the paved route replaces a rugged gravel climb with safe, year-round access.

Read the full story at omanspire.om (link in bio).
